anchor_receipts.actual_step_quote: Each supplied cusp group $P_i$ is the full stabilizer of its ideal point. By [F1] the full stabilizer is a translation lattice $Q_i$ containing $P_i$. Every translation in $Q_i$ preserves the entire source horoball. If some were outside $P_i$, two points of that horoball distinct modulo $P_i$ would have the same image in $M$, contradicting the supplied cusp embedding. Thus $P_i=Q_i$, and [F1] makes it maximal abelian. Conversely, let $A$ be any maximal abelian rank-two subgroup. Its proper embedded horocusp from [F1] has a connected tail missing the given compact core: properness makes its inverse image of that core compact. That tail lies in one of the finitely many supplied cusp components. Its inclusion on fundamental groups therefore puts $A$, up to conjugacy, inside that component's $P_i$. Maximality gives equality. In the compact case such a proper horocusp is impossible, so no rank-two abelian subgroup occurs. An isomorphism preserves abelianness, rank two and maximality, proving the peripheral assertion in both directions. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

The composites $GF$ and $FG$ are the identity on all sufficiently deep cusp tails. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. If $L_G,L_F\ge1$ are Lipschitz constants, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,x')\le2D+L_Gd(Fx,Fx')$, and similarly in the other direction. Thus $F$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and $d(FGy,y)\le D'$ proves coarse surjectivity. This proves the quasi-isometry assertion with explicit finite constants obtained from the constructed maps. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

For each matched cusp, choose upper half-space coordinates in source and target so that $\theta(P_i)$ is the corresponding target translation lattice, with any necessary conjugacy included in the choice of its lift. We prove the needed uniform small-matrix fact. In a neighborhood of the identity of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ choose the unique determinant-one lift near $I$, and put $\rho(g)=\max\{\|g-I\|,\|g^{-1}-I\|\}$ for a fixed matrix operator norm. For small $r$, the symmetric neighborhood $U_r=\{\rho<r\}$ has compact closure. Writing $g=I+X,h=I+Y$ gives $[g,h]-I=(XY-YX)g^{-1}h^{-1}$. The same formula with $g,h$ reversed bounds the inverse commutator, so $\rho([g,h])\le C\rho(g)\rho(h)$ on $U_r$, for one fixed $C$. Choose $r$ with $Cr\le1/2$. For any discrete subgroup $D$, the finite set $S=D\cap U_r$ generates a nilpotent subgroup. Indeed, every left-nested commutator of $n$ elements of $S$ has $\rho\le r2^{-(n-1)}$, by induction, and remains in $U_r$. Since the identity is isolated in $D$, all such commutators vanish for one common sufficiently large $n$. To justify the nilpotence conclusion, argue by induction on this common bound: the commutators of length $n-1$ commute with every generator, hence generate a central subgroup; quotient by it and use the induction hypothesis. The initial bound $n=1$ is the trivial group. Thus the group has a finite central series. Compactness makes $D\cap U_r$ finite, since a discrete subgroup is closed as in [F2]'s elementary proof. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

Such a $D$ preserves either a unique ideal point or a pair of ideal points, unless trivial. If $H$ is trivial, finite index and torsion-freeness make $D$ trivial. Otherwise its normal core in $D$ has finite index and is nontrivial and nilpotent. A nontrivial nilpotent group has a nontrivial center, by its central series; choose a central element $z$. Its centralizer from [F2] puts that normal core into either the translations fixing the parabolic point of $z$ or the diagonal group fixing its loxodromic pair. It is abelian and has that unique common fixed set. Normality makes $D$ preserve that set. A discrete torsion-free group preserving a pair is cyclic: an element interchanging the pair has order two, and the remaining diagonal group is cyclic by [F2]. A group preserving one point consists either of translations or is cyclic loxodromic. For the latter assertion, conjugate a loxodromic element fixing that point to a dilation fixing infinity and zero. Its commutator with any affine map fixing infinity is a translation. A nonzero such translation, conjugated by contracting powers of the dilation, tends to the identity, impossible in a discrete group. Thus all affine maps commute with the dilation and lie in the cyclic diagonal group. This proves the assertion and also that $D$ is abelian. By model homogeneity, the same $\eta$ works at every point. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

anchor_receipts.actual_step_quote: First use [F5] to write $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ with the standard cusp decompositions, identifying their deck groups with the fundamental groups and transporting $\theta$ accordingly. We verify the finite-Haar hypothesis of [F3], rather than infer it from a citation. Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ and $K=\mathrm{SO}(3)$, the stabilizer of a point in $\mathbb H^3$. The action identifies $G$ with the oriented orthonormal frame bundle: in the ball model an orientation-preserving isometry can send the center to any point by an upper half-space affine map after Cayley conjugation, and its stabilizer acts as every rotation; an isometry fixing a frame fixes each geodesic with its initial velocity and is the identity. Give $K$ normalized bi-invariant volume from the Ad-invariant inner product $-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. Integrating this probability measure on each frame fiber against hyperbolic volume defines a smooth positive measure on $G$. It is independent of the local frame section, since changes of section are rotations, and is left-$G$-invariant, since $G$ acts isometrically on the base and by rotations on the fibers. It is also right invariant: in left-invariant tangent coordinates the Jacobian of right translation is $|\det_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{Ad}(g^{-1})|$. On $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ the complex determinant of Ad is one. For diagonal matrices its eigenvalues are $a^2,1,a^{-2}$; for upper and lower unipotent matrices Ad is triangular with diagonal entries one. These matrices generate $G$ by Gaussian elimination, so the determinant assertion holds for every $g$. The real determinant is the squared modulus of the complex one. Thus the displayed frame measure is Haar on both sides. Its quotient on $\Gamma\backslash G$ is the locally transported right invariant Radon measure required in [F3]. Local product integration and a disjoint countable chart decomposition give its total mass exactly $\operatorname{Vol}(M)$, since the fiber mass is one. It is finite and positive. [A1, F5, given, algebra]

If nontrivial it gives, by conjugation with contracting powers, nontrivial elements tending to the identity. Thus all elements also fix the loxodromic element’s second endpoint, and the diagonal subgroup is cyclic by the compact-annulus argument. The translation case has rank at most two, by the elementary lattice proof in [F1]'s supplier. A subgroup preserving just a pair of ideal points is also cyclic: an element interchanging them has order two in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ and is excluded, and the remaining diagonal subgroup is cyclic by the compact-annulus argument in that same proof. All these quotients have infinite volume. For rank-two translations integrate $y^{-3}$ over a Euclidean fundamental parallelogram and $y\downarrow0$; rank-one translations have in addition an infinite horizontal direction. A cyclic loxodromic quotient has cylindrical density $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\varphi\,dt$ about its axis, with $t$ taken modulo its positive translation length, so integrating over $r\to\infty$ diverges even if its generator rotates the cylinder. The trivial quotient is $\mathbb H^3$ and has infinite volume as well. These direct integrations contradict the given finite volume. [F1, given, algebra]
